title: [YouPass Collect] - Australian math graduate employment and salary trends from 2004-2012
prompt: The graphs below show the percentage of math graduates and other graduates who got full-time job after graduating from a university in Australia, and also show the average salary of both these types of graduates, from 2004 to 2012. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

frame.name: Introduction
paragraphs: The line graph and table provide information about the employment rates and average salaries of mathematics graduates compared to graduates from other fields in Australia between 2004 and 2012.

frame.name: Overview
paragraphs: Overall, while employment figures for both groups fluctuated over the period, salaries increased consistently for both categories. Additionally, mathematics graduates generally enjoyed higher employment rates and earned more than their counterparts, although the gap in employment narrowed significantly in 2008.

frame.name: Body 1
paragraphs: Looking at the employment data, around 80% of maths graduates were in full-time employment in 2004, which was approximately 15 percentage points higher than the figure for other graduates, at roughly 65%. The proportion of employed maths graduates then rose sharply to a peak of about 90% in 2006, before declining steadily to approximately 80% by 2012. A similar pattern was observed among other graduates, whose employment rate climbed to just over 80% in 2006, peaked at close to 85% in 2008, and subsequently fell back to around 65% at the end of the period.

frame.name: Body 2
paragraphs: Regarding salaries, both groups started at an identical figure of $41,000 in 2004, which increased to $43,000 two years later. From 2008 onwards, however, maths graduates began earning more, with their average salary rising from $50,000 to $56,000 in 2012. Meanwhile, other graduates saw a smaller increase, from $45,000 to just over $50,000 over the same period, resulting in a wage gap of roughly $5,000 by the final year.
